newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rights curbs plan lays HK open to China meddling.
newsitem.headline: Rights curbs plan lays HK open to China meddling.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government has softened a contentious plan to curb civil liberties but legal analysts say the new laws will still lay the territory open to Chinese political meddling and suppression of dissent.

Bombarded with criticism at home and abroad, future leader Tung Chee-hwa announced the partial retreat on Thursday, narrowing a ban on foreign political funding and moderating previously planned limits on the right to protest.

The new version of the curbs will be processed on Saturday by a provisional legislature that is preparing to take over from Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council on July 1 after China reabsorbs the 156-year-old British colony as a special region.
"The justification for the changes has still simply not been made. The existing laws seemed totally adequate," Raymond Wacks, a law professor at Hong Kong University, told Reuters on Friday.
Wacks noted that the ban on foreign political funding meant the only groups outside Hong Kong who could donate money to Hong Kong political groups would be organisations in China.
"Clearly it gives mainland authorities an opportunity to exercise control over political life in Hong Kong," Wacks said.
Under the 1984 handover treaty, based on a "one country two systems" formula, Hong Kong will become virtually autonomous in all matters, except defence and diplomacy.
The tweaking of the planned laws gives police leeway to allow protest marches at short notice in exceptional instances, removing a previously planned minimum 48 hour notice rule.
And the restriction on foreign donations to political groups is confined to funds from "foreign political organisations".
"Mr Tung has given greater flexibility to demonstrators so they can go ahead even without the letter of no objection," said pro-China legislator Ronald Arculli, backing the restrictions.
The future government did not budge from a provision that will allow authorities to ban demonstrations or refuse the registration of societies on grounds of "national security".
"I don't think there's any substance in these latest changes to the original proposals," said Nihal Jayawickrama, an expert on law, politics and civil rights at Hong Kong University.
Jayawickrama said the revised plan retained the concept of "prior permission" for demonstrations, while simply tinkering with the time limit for notifying the police.
The clarification of the funding ban also meant very little. "It effectively still rules out any assistance from political groups anywhere except from China," he said.
"And national security has been retained as grounds for restrictions. It's aimed at controlling dissent, not external threats," Jayawickrama said.
Tung said in a speech on Thursday night he amended his original civil rights curbs after he had "listened carefully to public opinions on the document".
"I want to assure you that I am firmly committed to safeguarding the rights of the individual," he said.
He said the curbs were neeed to balance civil liberties against social order, comply with Hong Kong's future constitution, laid down by China in 1990, and prevent "foreign interference".
Pro-China legislator Ip Kwok-him said it was impossible to include China in the foreign funding ban. "We can understand why Mr Tung did not accept this idea because we are one country."
Britain has attacked the moves. "There is no justification for such amendments to the present laws," the government said.
"Local groups will be in danger," said Cheung Man-kwong, a spokesmam for Hong Kong's democracy movement.
"National security should not become a reason to restrict freedom," said Robyn Kilpatrick, head of the Hong Kong office of human rights group Amnesty International.
